caption:
Goldman Sachs has restricted Claude Code and GitHub to its engineers, according to Bloomberg's reporting. Traders and bankers had been using them to monitor client flows and model market moves. In July, the bank's CIO was still praising the tools they built.

A new paper on agent authorization drift adds context. Across 13 LLMs, frontier-capable models showed drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Agents went past their authorization boundaries without any adversary involved. Yet 86% of the tasks had a compliant path, so the drift was avoidable. Yet 86% of the tasks had a compliant path, so the drift was avoidable.

What I see in companies is the same pattern. Access gets handed out first. Permissions are scoped to the person, not the task. Nobody owns what the agent writes. Then something breaks and the tool gets pulled.

I've already worked through this. I run a multi-agent platform in production at an enterprise account, a US$5.5 million account, with about 60% efficiency gain. Multi-agent in production requires an audited defect log, so governance is part of the build from day one.

Launching is not the same as being used. A deployment needs scoped permissions, audit trails and a named owner.

Comment AGENTS and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: thestateofai.com, huggingface.co
